title: Architectural Decomposition
subtitle: Choose a migration path from evidence in the codebase
summary: Architectural decomposition explains how to break apart a monolith after modularity has supplied the reason. The first question is feasibility: can the codebase’s internal structure support controlled extraction? Coupling metrics help reveal that structure. Afferent coupling counts incoming connections, while efferent coupling counts outgoing connections. Abstractness and instability provide a broader view of how abstract and concrete code balance and how much a component depends outward. When code is structured into recognizable components, component-based decomposition can incrementally refine and extract them. When it is a Big Ball of Mud with little usable structure, tactical forking may be more pragmatic: clone the application, let teams remove unwanted behavior, and converge on coarse services. Both approaches carry trade-offs; the selection depends on evidence, not fashion or the elephant-migration instinct.

concepts.title: Decomposition is how
concepts.body: Modularity answers why a system should be partitioned; decomposition answers how to perform the work. The chapter warns that extracting pieces opportunistically can produce a distributed Big Ball of Mud. A deliberate process begins by asking whether the codebase is decomposable, then uses its internal structure to select component-based extraction or tactical forking.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: extracting knowledge-base code first may look easy, but without a boundary plan it can create new cross-service dependencies and a distributed monolith.

concepts.title: Big Ball of Mud
concepts.body: A Big Ball of Mud lacks useful internal structure: event handlers may reach directly into database calls, and boundaries are difficult to name or preserve. Before applying decomposition patterns, architects must assess whether the existing system is salvageable. The assessment is judgment informed by coupling tools, not a single magic score.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: a codebase where every screen imports every persistence class is a stronger candidate for tactical forking than careful component extraction.

concepts.title: Afferent and efferent
concepts.body: Afferent coupling measures incoming connections to an artifact; efferent coupling measures its outgoing connections. These counts expose shared assets that become risky during extraction. A class such as Address may be easy to reuse inside a monolith yet difficult to separate when many candidate services depend on it.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: a shared customer formatter with many incoming uses deserves explicit treatment before it is moved across a service boundary.

concepts.title: Two migration paths
concepts.body: Component-based decomposition refactors and extracts logical components incrementally, commonly moving toward a service-based architecture. Tactical forking copies the monolith and removes unwanted parts from each copy, preserving coarse behavior where structure is too poor for extraction. Forking can be pragmatic, but duplicated code and later convergence are real costs.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: two teams can fork a mud-like system into ticketing and reporting slices, then retire unused screens and reconcile shared contracts.

misconceptions.claim: The easiest feature to extract should always be extracted first.
misconceptions.correction: An unstructured sequence can create a distributed monolith; choose a method after assessing code structure and coupling.

misconceptions.claim: One coupling metric decides whether decomposition is possible.
misconceptions.correction: Afferent and efferent measures, abstractness, instability, and architectural judgment together inform feasibility.

scenario.title: Choose the migration path
scenario.context: The ticketing system has a large reporting component but also many direct UI-to-database calls and shared utility classes. The team must start a funded migration while limiting the risk of creating distributed mud. It can use component extraction where boundaries are visible and tactical forking where they are not.

options.label: Component path
options.benefit: Preserves incremental control and makes dependencies explicit as components are refined.
options.cost: Requires analysis and refactoring before visible service separation.
options.consequence: Reporting is decomposed along clear domains, while high-coupling utilities are redesigned before extraction.

options.label: Tactical fork
options.benefit: Provides a pragmatic start when the codebase lacks reliable internal structure.
options.cost: Duplicates code and creates convergence and governance work across copies.
options.consequence: Teams remove unrelated behavior from ticket and reporting copies, then must reconcile shared fixes and retire duplication.

scenario.debrief: The choice follows evidence about structure. Extraction rewards coherent components; forking limits the need to understand every tangled dependency but carries duplicated-system costs.

quiz.question: What does afferent coupling count?
quiz.explanation: Afferent is incoming; efferent is outgoing.

quiz.question: When is tactical forking most appropriate?
options: When components are already cleanly bounded
When the codebase has little usable internal structure
quiz.explanation: Forking is presented as a pragmatic approach for Big Balls of Mud.

quiz.question: What is the first decomposition question?
quiz.explanation: Feasibility and internal structure precede selecting an approach or target topology.

exercise.title: Assess a codebase
exercise.prompt: Use a small dependency sample to decide whether component extraction or tactical forking is safer, and justify the choice.

steps.text: Inspect boundaries, shared assets, and direct dependencies.
Compare incoming and outgoing coupling and broader structural signals.
Choose incremental component extraction when boundaries are usable.
Choose tactical forking when the structure is too tangled to extract safely.
